title: Shift and Affine Ciphers
short: Encrypt letters with x ↦ ax + b (mod 26) and decrypt with x ↦ a⁻¹(x − b); a must be coprime to 26.
trouble: Students decrypt by subtracting b and dividing by a as ordinary numbers instead of multiplying by the inverse of a mod 26.

blocks.html: Secret codes are the oldest application of modular arithmetic. Number the letters $A = 0, B = 1, \dots, Z = 25$ and calculate mod 26. Encrypting is multiplying and adding; decrypting is undoing that, which needs a modular inverse.

Shift cipher (Caesar's): $E(x) = x + b \bmod 26$, undone by $D(y) = y - b$. Affine cipher: $$E(x) = ax + b \bmod 26, \qquad D(y) = a^{-1}(y - b) \bmod 26.$$ The key is the pair $(a, b)$, and $a$ must satisfy $\gcd(a, 26) = 1$.

To undo $y \equiv ax + b$, subtract $b$ and then "divide by $a$", which mod 26 means multiplying by $a^{-1}$: $a^{-1}(y - b) \equiv a^{-1} a x = x$. The inverse exists exactly when $\gcd(a, 26) = 1$, that is, $a$ is odd and not 13. Those 12 values of $a$ and 26 values of $b$ give $12 \cdot 26 = 312$ keys. If $\gcd(a, 26) > 1$, two letters are sent to the same place, and the message can no longer be read back.

blocks.title: A bad key
steps: $13 \cdot 0 = 0$ and $13 \cdot 2 = 26 \equiv 0$, so A and C get the same cipher letter (for any $b$).
In fact $13x \bmod 26$ is only ever $0$ or $13$, so the cipher uses just two letters.

head: $a$
blocks.cap: The allowed multipliers and their inverses mod 26.

blocks.html: Decrypting by ordinary division: "$x = (y - 8)/5$." For Q $= 16$, that gives $8/5$, not a letter. Mod 26, dividing by 5 means multiplying by $5^{-1} = 21$. Check any decryption by encrypting it again.

An affine cipher is also weak against a known-plaintext attack: if Eve learns that two plaintext letters $x_1, x_2$ encrypt to $y_1, y_2$, she solves the two congruences $ax_1 + b \equiv y_1$ and $ax_2 + b \equiv y_2$. Subtracting gives $a(x_1 - x_2) \equiv y_1 - y_2 \pmod{26}$, a linear congruence for $a$, and then $b$ follows.

With only 312 keys, an affine cipher falls to a computer instantly, and even by hand to letter-frequency counting (E is the most common letter in English). Modern cryptography keeps the modular arithmetic but uses enormous moduli and keys that never have to be shared, as in RSA.
Affine cipher: $E(x) = ax + b \bmod 26$ with $\gcd(a, 26) = 1$; decrypt with $D(y) = a^{-1}(y - b)$, using the inverse of $a$ mod 26.
